rows.label: Formula
rows.text: Longitudinal chromatic aberration: $f_r - f_v = \omega f$, where $\omega$ is the lens's dispersive power.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).  ·  **Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Chromatic aberration is caused by dispersion (wavelength-dependent $n$); spherical aberration is caused by the spherical shape of the lens surface. They are fundamentally different phenomena that both degrade image quality.  ·  Stopping down (using a diaphragm) reduces spherical aberration by blocking marginal rays, but it does NOT reduce chromatic aberration — all rays, regardless of height, still experience the same dispersion.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: A single lens always disperses; only a combination of two glasses can recombine the colours at one focus.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: All simple spherical lenses suffer from both chromatic and spherical aberration — no single spherical lens can form a perfect image.  ·  The Hubble Space Telescope's initial primary mirror had a spherical aberration of about 2.2 micrometres — a tiny error that produced blurry images because of the mirror's 2.4-metre diameter.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Chromatic aberration:** a lens fails to focus all colours at the same point because $n$ varies with wavelength. Violet (higher $n$) focuses closer to the lens than red (lower $n$), producing coloured fringes around images.  ·  **Spherical aberration:** rays passing through the edge (marginal rays) of a spherical lens focus at a different point from rays passing through the centre (paraxial rays). Marginal rays focus closer to the lens because the surface curvature is steeper at the edges.  ·  **Why spherical aberration occurs:** the lens surface is part of a sphere, but the ideal focusing surface for parallel rays is a paraboloid, not a sphere. A spherical surface is only an approximation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Chromatic and spherical aberration and other topics  ·  **Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.  ·  A plano-convex lens does not eliminate spherical aberration entirely; it only minimizes it for a particular object distance. Only a parabolic surface eliminates it completely for collimated light.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Spherical aberration affects all wavelengths equally (monochromatic aberration), while chromatic aberration affects different wavelengths differently (polychromatic aberration).  ·  Using a thinner lens does not eliminate either aberration — it only reduces the magnitude. The fundamental cause (spherical shape for spherical aberration, dispersion for chromatic aberration) remains.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Chromatic and spherical aberration
